title: What’s the Pinglu Canal, China’s new gateway to Southeast Asia?
description: China's first modern river-to-sea canal could significantly cut down time and costs of trade to Southeast Asia.
content: Beijing, China – China is opening its first modern river-to-sea canal for navigation on Wednesday, a project that aims to dramatically cut down shipping distances between the country’s southern hinterland and Southeast Asia, a region that serves as a critical trade partner. The Pinglu Canal is located entirely in Guangxi, the region in China’s far south bordering Vietnam and overlooking the South China Sea. This 134km (83-mile) waterway links the Xijiang River with the Beibu Gulf, the northwestern arm of the Gulf of Tonkin stretching between southern China and northern Vietnam. It gives vast areas of southwest China, including provinces such as Yunnan and Guizhou, a shorter route to the sea and to Asian markets. The first such canal built by communist China, Pinglu is a part of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor: A project involving southern Chinese provinces aimed at linking areas in western and southwestern China with Southeast Asian countries and global markets. The land-sea trade corridor is itself a part of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative, a web of highways, ports and railroads seeking to connect China with Europe and Africa. The real gain: Savings in distance and cost According to local authorities in Guangxi, the canal will shorten the shipping distance between inland areas of southwest China and Southeast Asian countries by about 560km (350 miles) and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent. Estimates by Zhang Zhiwen, deputy secretary-general of the Guangxi government, indicate that transport costs alone will come down by more than 5 billion yuan annually, or about $700m. The region’s vice chairwoman, Lu Xinning, describes these returns as “tangible gains” that reduce operating costs and boost domestic and foreign trade. The canal will allow the passage of ships with a capacity of 5,000 tonnes. Its estimated cost is about 72.7 billion yuan, equivalent to about $10.8bn. This means cities and industrial areas far from the coast in southwest China will become closer to maritime trade routes. The new trade corridor does not serve Guangxi alone; it is connected to a broader network extending to Chongqing in southwest China, Chengdu in Sichuan province, Guizhou and Yunnan, before goods reach the ports of the Beibu Gulf and, from there, overseas markets. These changes come at a time when trade between China and Southeast Asia is growing rapidly. According to China’s General Administration of Customs, bilateral trade in the first half of 2026 reached about 4.34 trillion yuan, or about $640bn, an increase of 18.2 percent year on year. At the southern end of the canal, container-handling capacity at Beibu Gulf Port rose from 2.28 million TEUs in 2017 to 10.06 million TEUs in 2025, with a shipping network covering major Southeast Asian ports. From waterway to industrial hub Guangxi is also working to build what it calls the “Pinglu Canal Economic Belt”, with the aim of attracting industries and spreading them out along the new corridor, while linking them to ports, transport networks and supply chains. The targeted sectors include non-ferrous metals and critical minerals, modern green chemicals, as well as artificial intelligence and information technology. Industrial zones are also being developed near ports, reducing the distance between production sites and shipping centres. The process of organising and directing shipping sources has already begun to generate new commercial activity. A train loaded with sodium bisulfate recently arrived from Chongqing, the major industrial and transport hub in southwest China, at the port of Nanning, the capital of Guangxi province. After the canal opens, direct commercial sailings are scheduled to begin to the port of Can Tho in southern Vietnam. On the operational front, Guangxi has adopted a tiered transit-fee system that gives operators a grace period before imposing nominal charges. Until December 31, 2026, commercial vessels will pass through the three water gates along the canal completely free of charge. Starting January 1, 2027, a fee of one yuan, about $0.14, will be charged for each tonne of a vessel’s capacity every time it passes through these gates. This trial rate will remain in effect until September 2031. River vessels can sail directly to the berths of Qinzhou seaport without needing to transfer their cargo to other ships, enabling a seamless transition from river to sea. Resettlement: Another side of the canal project Building a canal of this scale would not have been possible without addressing a sensitive human dimension: Relocating thousands of families from their land. According to official sources, the resettlement process involved 2,764 households comprising 11,228 people across four counties and county-level cities in Guangxi. In Hengzhou alone, evacuation agreements were signed for 368 homes, which were completely demolished over a total area of 84,200 square metres (906,321 square feet), with 1,221 people temporarily resettled. The process was not managed solely through financial compensation. Instead, 21 different housing models were designed in accordance with residents’ customs: The orientation of reception rooms, crop-drying areas, poultry enclosures and storage rooms for agricultural chemicals. In Shaping, the largest town in the resettlement project, residents were given four-storey homes covering 420sq metres (4,520sq ft), some with commercial storefronts facing the street. Still, there is a sense of loss among many, even if mitigated by hope for the future. In Xinfu, where the village of Fenghuangping once stood, one resident who was forced to leave said: “There is no longer a village called Fenghuangping, but with the Pinglu Canal, tomorrow will be better.” Some families moved seven-century-old trees to the new site of their homes, including a 217-year-old camphor tree. The resettlement process was carried out within 39 days, but it was linked to promises of jobs at the construction site and vocational training for residents of the relocated areas. How geography is reshaping trade security Straits and maritime corridors have long been the arteries of power in the global economy, but they are also among its most sensitive points of weakness. The Hormuz crisis embodies this paradox: The passageway through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow can, when threatened, become a factor that paralyses trade and redraws its routes. Faced with that backdrop, countries around the world are trying to develop alternative routes and supply chains – pipelines, storage facilities and transport corridors that reduce the dependence of nations on just one or two routes. The Pinglu Canal is China’s latest endeavour to do just that: Build an alternative, shorter and faster route to a critical market.

title: Indian economy at inflection point, needs growth rethink: CEA Nageswaran
description: Nageswaran argued that India needs to rethink its development model for the AI era, using artificial intelligence to boost workers rather than replace them
content: Indian economy at inflection point, needs growth rethink: CEA Nageswaran Nageswaran argued that India needs to rethink its development model for the AI era, using artificial intelligence to boost workers rather than replace them Listen to This Article By Anup Roy India’s economy is at an “inflection point” that requires the country to rethink policies that powered its growth over the past three decades, according to Chief Economic Advisor Anantha Nageswaran. “This is a period of churn and this is an inflection point,” Nageswaran said at an event in New Delhi on Tuesday. What served the country well since it gained independence from the British colonial rule “may not necessarily be adequate for the next 25 years,” Nageswaran said. “We need to raise our game in multiple respects.” Nageswaran argued that India needs to rethink its development model for the AI era, using artificial intelligence to boost workers rather than replace them and avoiding the capital-intensive model pursued by richer economies. Also Read The country’s youth should be open to acquiring trade skills rather than relying solely on conventional education as artificial intelligence reshapes employment, he added. “We have to find ways in which we use AI to complement rather than displace labor, because we are a large country,” he said. Nageswaran expressed confidence in India’s economy amid geopolitical tensions and high crude oil prices, pointing to strong bank credit growth, tax collections and healthy corporate and banking sector balance sheets. The economy grew a solid 7.8% in the April-June quarter. “The private sector must invest, must hire and must compensate fairly and also invest in R&D because the next 20 years is going to be very different from the last 80 years post World War II,” he said. title: Houthis 'fire drone at Mecca' and 'shoot down Saudi fighter jet' as war intensifies
description: Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree was quick to dismiss Saudi claims that the group had targeted Mecca, after widespread condemnation.
content: - See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source The Houthis have been accused of launching a drone towards the holy city of Mecca, while the militant group claims to have shot down a Saudi fighter jet amid escalating conflict across the region. The developments come as fears are growing of a new global oil supply crisis after Houthi rebels seized the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish in the southern Red Sea after attacking a Saudi pipeline. The Iran-backed group have been fighting a civil war in Yemen against a Saudi-led coalition since 2014. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to shift its exports away from the Persian Gulf, since Iranian attacks have stifled shipping through the gulf's sole exit, the Strait of Hormuz. And on Tuesday morning, Brent crude rose 1.17 per cent to $106.92 a barrel, while the average US diesel price last week surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time as the war, compounded by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, further squeezed global supplies. Meanwhile in the UK, rises in petrol, diesel and airfares has pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in five months due to disruptions from the war in Iran. Inflation rose to 3.1 per cent from 2.9 per cent, according to the Office for National Statistics. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree was quick to dismiss Saudi claims that the group had targeted Mecca, after widespread condemnation. Mecca is regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and is the holiest city in Islam 'Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,' he said. Mecca is regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and is the holiest city in Islam. Muslims who are physically and financially able are required to make the pilgrimage to the city at least once in their lifetime, with millions travelling there each year. Major General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition Forces, condemned the attempted attack on X, writing: 'This hostile attempt will also remain a black mark in the record of violations by the extremist terrorist Houthi militia, as a deliberate act intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.' He vowed to take any 'necessary and deterrent measures' against the group. And the Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming a locally made munition was used to target the warplane. 'The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military mobilisations in the airspace of Marib province,' Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes. He said the jet had been targeted 'using a locally made air-to-air missile'. Saudi Arabia has relied on the East-West Pipeline, which runs 1,200km (124 miles) across the breadth of the country, to move its crude production from Gulf ports to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. From there it can be put on tankers for export. But authorities were forced to shut down the pipeline after an attack on Thursday that Saudi Arabia blamed on drones from Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. Repairing the damage, including at a major pumping facility, could take three to five weeks, officials have said. The pipeline may work partially during the repairs, one of the officials said, but they could not say how much oil might get through. The pipeline has been moving an average of 2.6 million to four million barrels per day since late August – a quantity that will be lost to the market if the pipeline's flow stops completely, according to an analysis issued Monday by Rystad Energy, a Norway-based research firm. Meanwhile, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels continued to expand their threat to Saudi shipping routes out of the Red Sea by capturing the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, government and Houthi officials said Monday. The islands lie 160km (99 miles) north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait is a choke point that connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and Saudi Arabia's key Asian markets. The Houthis' advance also puts them just 20 miles from the US military base in the tiny Horn of Africa nation of Djibouti, on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. For more than a month, the Houthis have been striking Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, stepping up pressure on global oil prices and boosting Iran's leverage in its war with the US. Houthi threats have kept the Kingdom on high alert, with air raid warnings sounding across the country daily, while a series of ballistic missile and drone attacks by the group wounded 13 civilians on Monday. The rebels deployed on the Hanish islands after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official. Last week, the rebels seized the port city of Mokha and the island of Mayun, inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Government forces are now attempting to rally and fight back. On Sunday, the military said it launched airstrikes on Houthi positions in Mokha, the coastal town of Dhubab and elsewhere in Taiz province. A combination of satellite images shows the Saudi Arabia East-West pipeline before (top) and after (bottom) attacks Supporters of Yemen's Houthi rebels chant and raise rifles during a rally organized to celebrate the group's capture of Mayun Island on September 11 A rebel spokesman said the Houthis fired dozens of missiles and drones at the King Khalid Airbase in the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, targeting hangars, radar installations and ammunition depots. The statement on Monday by Saree did not specify when the strikes took place but the Houthis often take hours or days to claim responsibility for attacks. General al-Maliki said the attacks struck civilian areas in Khamis Mushait and other nearby cities, injuring 13 civilians and damaging several houses and vehicles. He did not say whether the airbase had been hit. The Iran war has gouged Saudi oil production, which was down to six million barrels per day in August from nearly ten million in September the previous year, according to the International Energy Agency. The fighting has also displaced nearly 94,000 people in Yemen who have since fled their homes. 'Many of them don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied,' said Khanzad Shah, acting head of Islamic Relief, a charity that operates in the area. Around 200 schools have been converted to shelters in southwestern Yemen to absorb an influx of families, said Basma Alloush, deputy director of communications at the International Rescue Committee, an aid group.

title: In 1854, a 16-word message from Kolkata to Bengaluru cost 10 shillings; how Bengaluru’s telegraph era lasted until 2013
description: Bengaluru joined India's electric telegraph network in 1854, transforming communication speed. A 16-word message between Calcutta and Bengaluru cost ten shillings then. This new technology connected Bengaluru to Madras, Bellary, and Bombay. Later, a line to M…
content: Today, a message can travel from Bengaluru to almost anywhere in the world in seconds. But in the mid-19th century, sending information across long distances was a far more complicated and expensive affair. In 1854, Bengaluru became part of India's expanding electric telegraph network. The city's telegraph office opened on May 23, 1854, giving residents access to a technology that could transmit messages far faster than traditional methods of communication. A 16-word message between Calcutta (now Kolkata) and Bengaluru cost 10 shillings at the time, according to a historical chronology of Bengaluru, as per multiple reports. The price reflected how new and specialised the technology was in its early years. The wires that connected Bengaluru to bigger cities Bengaluru's telegraph connection was part of a larger line running from Madras towards Bellary, passing through the city. The network was later extended towards Bombay, placing Bengaluru on a route that connected several important centres in southern and western India. The expansion was part of the rapid development of electric telegraphy across India in the 1850s. William O'Shaughnessy, who had conducted some of the earliest experiments with electric telegraphy in India, played a major role in developing the system. Work on long-distance telegraph lines accelerated in the early 1850s. By March 1854, an electric telegraph connection between Calcutta and Agra had been established, and the network continued expanding to other major cities and towns. An account of the early Indian telegraph network published in the period noted the speed with which messages could be transmitted over long distances, making the technology particularly valuable at a time when travelling between cities could take days. Bengaluru's link with Mysore came a year later The telegraph network around Bengaluru expanded quickly. In March 1855, a telegraph line connecting Bengaluru with Mysore was established and a telegraph office was opened in Mysore. The Bengaluru historical chronology records the line as being 84 miles long, with the establishment of the two offices costing over Rs 8,000. The new connection gave Bengaluru another important communication link — this time with Mysore, the capital of the princely state. By then, the city was becoming part of a much wider network in which information could move without waiting for a person or a physical document to travel between cities. From messages carried by hand to messages sent through wires Before the telegraph, communicating over long distances generally meant relying on people or physical transport to carry information. The electric telegraph changed that equation. A message could be converted into electrical signals, sent through wires and decoded at the other end For Bengaluru, this meant that information could travel along the city's growing connections to Madras, Bellary, Bombay and Mysore. The technology also arrived at a time when Bengaluru itself was changing. Railways would follow in the next decade. In 1864, the city got its first railway connection when a line between Bengaluru Cantonment and Jolarpettai opened, creating another faster link with the wider region. Together, the telegraph and railway gradually reduced the isolation of a city whose communication and transport had previously depended heavily on slower methods. The telegraph's long life in Bengaluru The technology that began with messages priced by the word eventually became an ordinary part of communication in Bengaluru. Telegrams were used for everything from urgent personal messages to business communication, particularly when a fast written message was needed. The service remained in use in the city for more than a century and a half. Telegram service was finally discontinued in 2013, bringing an end to a system that had begun in Bengaluru in the 1850s. At the time of the shutdown, multiple reports said Bengaluru had 21 telegraph offices. What began in 1854 with a costly 16-word message had thus become part of the city's communication infrastructure for generations — long before Bengaluru's present-day reputation for connecting people through phones, computers and the internet.

title: Improvement in economic indicators points to Nigeria’s stabilisation — UBA boss
description: Group Managing Director of United Bank for Africa (UBA) and Chairman of the Body of Bank CEOs in Nigeria, Oliver Alawuba, has outlined a blueprint for building a resilient Nigerian economy, calling for deliberate policies and stronger collaboration across the…
content: Group Managing Director of United Bank for Africa (UBA) and Chairman of the Body of Bank CEOs in Nigeria, Oliver Alawuba, has outlined a blueprint for building a resilient Nigerian economy, calling for deliberate policies and stronger collaboration across the public and private sectors to transform economic stability into inclusive prosperity. Alawuba made the call while delivering his goodwill speech at the 19th Annual Banking and Finance Conference of the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN), held in Abuja last week. Speaking on the theme of the conference, “Building a Resilient Economy in an Era of Disruptions: Imperatives for the Banking and Financial Services Industry,” Alawuba said resilience must be deliberately designed into Nigeria’s policies, institutions, infrastructure, supply chains, energy systems, financial architecture and human capital. According to him, a resilient economy is not one that never encounters shocks, but one that can absorb, adapt and advance without transferring the full cost of every disruption to its most vulnerable citizens. He noted that the global economy continues to face structural disruptions, from geopolitical conflicts and volatility in energy and shipping markets to inflationary pressures, making it imperative for Nigeria to build systems capable of withstanding future shocks rather than responding only after they occur. Alawuba commended the Federal Government and the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) for the increasingly effective coordination between fiscal and monetary policy, noting that recent improvements in key economic indicators provide important milestones in Nigeria’s stabilisation journey. He also stressed that these gains must now be translated into broader economic opportunities and improved living standards and further highlighted the critical role of the banking industry in Nigeria’s resilience agenda, describing banks as the country’s “financial shock absorbers and growth partners.” The UBA boss, pointed to the ₦4.65 trillion mobilised by 33 banks during the recent recapitalisation exercise as a significant step towards strengthening capital adequacy, asset quality, balance-sheet transparency and investor confidence, while expanding the industry’s capacity to absorb shocks and finance larger projects. According to Alawuba, the banking sector’s resilience is being reinforced by accelerated investment in digital infrastructure, cybersecurity and operational resilience, citing technology investments of over N119 billion by four leading banks in the first quarter of 2026, representing a 43.2 per cent year-on-year increase.

title: UPI MDR vs credit card, net banking: Do you pay extra for using them?
description: The new UPI MDR will apply to merchant payments above Rs 2,000 from October 15. For customers, the real cost difference still depends more on platform fees, convenience charges and card borrowing costs.
content: UPI MDR vs credit card, net banking: Do you pay extra for using them? The new UPI MDR will apply to merchant payments above Rs 2,000 from October 15. For customers, the real cost difference still depends more on platform fees, convenience charges and card borrowing costs. From October 15, paying a merchant through UPI for more than Rs 2,000 will carry a new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.4%, subject to a cap of Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. But there is an important catch: the customer is not supposed to pay this MDR. The charge will be levied within the merchant payment ecosystem, while banks have been advised to ensure merchants do not pass it on to customers. UPI app providers have also been barred from imposing platform fees or hidden charges on UPI payments. This raises a more interesting question for consumers, which is, if UPI remains free, how does it compare with credit cards and net banking? And when you see a "convenience fee", "platform fee" or other payment charge while booking a flight, buying a ticket or making an online purchase, does the payment method really make a difference? The answer is more nuanced than simply saying that one payment mode is cheaper. WHAT DOES THE NEW UPI MDR MEAN? The new 0.4% MDR applies to specified person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000 from October 15. A Rs 5,000 payment would mean an MDR of Rs 20 for the merchant. A Rs 50,000 payment would mean Rs 200. Once the transaction reaches Rs 75,000, the MDR is capped at Rs 300. The government has said this does not change the cost for consumers. Person-to-person UPI transfers remain free regardless of the amount, while payments to merchants up to Rs 2,000 remain free. Small merchants receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month through UPI QR codes also remain under the zero-MDR framework. The government estimates that around 96% of P2M transactions will remain unaffected by the new MDR. There are also special rates for some categories. Payments above Rs 2,000 to sectors such as railways, telecom, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs will attract a flat Rs 5 MDR, while capital-market transactions will attract 0.02%, capped at Rs 300. So, for a customer standing at a shop and paying Rs 10,000 through a UPI QR code, the 0.4% MDR does not mean an additional Rs 40 will be deducted from the customer's bank account. CREDIT CARD MDR IS ALSO NOT A CUSTOMER CHARGE This is where the comparison gets interesting. Credit-card transactions also involve MDR. But the merchant, rather than the customer, generally bears that cost. ICICI Bank, for instance, explains that merchants typically bear credit-card swipe charges. It says these can be around 2% for physical transactions and 2.3-2.5% for online transactions, although the actual rate depends on the arrangement. SBI's current account information shows negotiated or concessional domestic credit-card MDR rates ranging from 1% to 1.6% across certain account tiers. Its Platinum Current Account, for instance, lists 1.20% for domestic credit-card transactions, subject to the specified conditions and monthly limits. HDFC Bank says MDR for card payments is generally around 2-3%, while also noting that merchants can negotiate rates depending on their expected transaction volumes. The important point for consumers is that the MDR a merchant pays is not automatically a fee that appears on the customer's bill. For a normal Rs 10,000 credit-card purchase, a customer would generally see a Rs 10,000 transaction rather than Rs 10,000 plus a separate 2% "MDR charge". However, merchants can have different pricing or fee policies, and the cost of accepting cards can also indirectly influence the prices businesses charge. THEN WHY DO CUSTOMERS SOMETIMES SEE A PAYMENT FEE? This is where the story should go beyond MDR. A merchant can have other charges associated with a transaction that are separate from MDR. These could include a convenience fee, booking fee, platform fee or other service-related charge, depending on the product and the platform. RBI's framework for payment gateways and aggregators specifically distinguishes MDR from other charges such as convenience fees and says such charges, if levied, should be displayed to the customer before payment. RBI's credit-card rules also define a convenience fee as a fixed or percentage-based charge associated with using cards as an alternative payment method and require such fees to be disclosed transparently before a transaction. That distinction matters. MDR: generally a cost in the merchant-payment ecosystem. Convenience fee: a separate charge that can be imposed on the customer for a particular service or transaction, subject to applicable rules and disclosure. Platform/service fee: another possible charge associated with using a particular platform or service. So a customer may not be paying the merchant's MDR, but could still pay a separate convenience or service fee. NET BANKING CAN ALSO BE CHEAP — SOMETIMES FREE Net banking complicates the "UPI is cheaper" argument even further. RBI has directed banks not to levy charges on NEFT funds transfers initiated online by savings-bank account holders. That means if a consumer is simply transferring money from a savings account using online NEFT, the transaction itself may not cost anything. The actual cost can depend on the bank, account type and payment route. And this is where net banking differs from UPI. A net-banking transfer is primarily a bank-account transfer, while UPI is designed to work as a merchant payment interface as well. So a customer may have a Rs 0 direct transaction cost with both UPI and online NEFT, but the experience and availability at checkout can be very different. LOOK AT THE PAYMENT PAGE A useful example comes from IRCTC. Its published payment-provider charges show that the customer-facing cost can vary substantially by payment method. In one listed arrangement, UPI transactions carry no transaction charge, while domestic credit cards attract a percentage-based charge and net banking carries a fixed Rs 10 charge, with applicable taxes. The exact charge varies depending on the payment provider. This demonstrates why consumers cannot simply compare MDR percentages and conclude that one payment method always costs less. The merchant may be absorbing the MDR. But a platform can separately charge the customer for providing a payment or booking service, depending on its terms. Air India provides another example of a different kind of charge. It says its convenience fee is charged on bookings made through its website, app or call centres and applies across payment modes, rather than being tied specifically to UPI or credit cards. That distinction is important because a customer could switch from a credit card to UPI and still pay the same convenience fee. So which payment method is actually cheaper? There is no single answer because there are two different questions: what does the merchant pay, and what does the customer pay? For a straightforward shop purchase, UPI can remain a zero-direct-charge option for the customer even after October 15, because the new MDR is not supposed to be passed on. Credit cards can also have zero direct transaction charges at checkout, even though the merchant pays MDR. Net banking can also be free for certain online bank transfers, particularly NEFT initiated online by savings-account customers. The difference emerges when a platform adds a customer-facing charge. A customer booking a ticket could therefore see a convenience fee irrespective of whether UPI or a credit card is selected. Another platform could charge a fixed payment fee for net banking but nothing for UPI. A third could have different charges for different card types. CREDIT CARDS HAVE ANOTHER COST THAT UPI DOES NOT There is also a cost that does not appear at the moment of payment: the cost of borrowing. If a customer pays a credit-card bill in full by the due date, the purchase itself does not necessarily attract interest. But if the customer carries an outstanding balance, credit-card interest and other applicable charges can make the payment substantially more expensive. RBI requires card issuers to disclose interest rates and the methodology for calculating finance charges, including examples for situations where only part of the outstanding amount is paid. Credit cards can also carry annual fees, late-payment charges and charges for certain services. These are costs of having or using the credit facility rather than MDR. This means a consumer comparing payment modes should not look only at the fee displayed on the checkout page. DON'T CONFUSE MDR WITH YOUR PAYMENT COST The new UPI MDR changes the economics for merchants, but it does not currently turn UPI into a paid service for consumers. A customer paying a merchant Rs 20,000 through UPI will not suddenly see an additional Rs 80 MDR deducted from their account. The merchant bears the MDR under the new framework, and banks have been advised to prevent the cost from being passed on. But consumers can still encounter convenience fees, platform fees or other service charges depending on the merchant and the transaction. Those charges are separate from MDR and need to be checked before payment. Credit cards, meanwhile, can offer rewards, cashback or payment flexibility while the merchant bears the MDR. Net banking can be free for certain bank transfers but may attract a payment fee when used through particular merchant platforms.

title: Maharashtra FDA suspends Cafe Mondegar licence over food safety violations
description:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday said it has suspended the licences of Cafe Mondegar, a popular restaurant, and three other food establishments in Mumbai after inspections found serious food safety and hygiene violations.
The FDA …
content: Maharashtra FDA suspends Cafe Mondegar licence over food safety violations The FDA inspected Cafe Mondegar at Metro House in Colaba on September 12 and found serious deficiencies in safety and hygiene Listen to This Article The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Tuesday said it has suspended the licences of Cafe Mondegar, a popular restaurant, and three other food establishments in Mumbai after inspections found serious food safety and hygiene violations. The FDA inspected Cafe Mondegar at Metro House in Colaba on September 12 and found serious deficiencies in safety and hygiene, including failure to keep hot food above the prescribed 60 degrees Celsius and cold storage below 5 degrees Celsius, the regulator said in a release. Officials found improper thawing of food, inadequate rapid cooling of cooked food and sanitation and structural deficiencies at the restaurant that posed a risk of cross-contamination. The state agency also suspended the licences of Maharashtra Biryani Centre in Kandivali East, Tribhuvan Dairy Farm in Ghatkopar West and Mahavir Cashew & Foods Pvt Ltd in Ghatkopar East after inspections found violations of Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Standards Act. Schedule 4 of the Act prescribes mandatory hygiene and sanitation rules that all food business operators must follow. Also Read The FDA, which under new commissioner Tukaram Mundhe, has intensified its crackdown on safety, adulteration, and hygiene violations, said it also took action against nine food establishments in Mumbai for deficiencies found during inspections conducted as part of its festival season drive. These establishments include Ruhafza Bakery in Khar West; Chandru's Pure Ghee Sweets and Sharma Dairy & Fast Food in Andheri West; Punjabi Chandu Halwai LLP at Grant Road East; Shri Narayan Dairy in Vile Parle West; and Gulshan Dairy Farm in Khar West. The regulator said it inspected 38 food establishments in the metropolis and collected 47 food samples, including those of milk, khoya (creamy dairy product), ghee and sweets, for analysis during the special festival campaign between September 11-14. At Ayush Milk Supplier in Andheri East, officials collected a sample of sweet barfi and seized the remaining 23 kg stock, valued at ₹6,440. At Brijwasi Mithaiyan Shop in Mulund West, they collected a khoya sample and seized 225 kg of the remaining stock, valued at ₹60,300. The FDA also took action against several milk and milk-product establishments across Maharashtra. At Shivaratna Milk & Milk Agro Product in Takawade, Kolhapur, officials found 10 kg of halwa worth ₹6,000 and 198 kg of rabadi worth ₹45,540, both suspected to be substandard. At Creamy Delight in Patas, Pune, officials found 1,519 kg of cow milk, butter, and skimmed milk powder worth ₹8.50 lakh with labelling deficiencies and suspected substandard quality. At Mahaveer Dairy in Manchar, Pune, officials found 49 kg of khoya worth ₹13,720, 104 kg of paneer worth ₹31,200 and 11 kg of ghee worth ₹7,920, all suspected to be substandard. The FDA said it was initiating further legal action in these cases. In Jalgaon district, the food regulator seized around 2,155 kg of suspected adulterated sweet halwa worth ₹5.58 lakh from two transport vehicles. It also seized 28 kg of suspected substandard khoya worth ₹12,600 from Brijvilas Dairy in Jalgaon, 16.2 kg of suspected substandard 'peda' (sweet) and buffalo ghee worth ₹15,200 from Ekta Dudh Dairy and Sweets in Raver, and 6.5 kg of peda worth ₹2,600 from Tarachand Sundarji and Sons in Chalisgaon (Jalgaon district). Officials also found 19 kg of shrikhand worth ₹5,320 stored in unhygienic conditions at a premises belonging to one Samadhan Pawar, said the release. The FDA said it found 30 litres of loose pasteurised standardised buffalo milk, valued at ₹2,830, being sold at Bhairavnath Dairy in Badlapur, Thane, in violation of an order dated July 3, 2026. At Ayush Milk Supplier in Andheri East, officials found improper storage and inadequate or incorrect labelling of sweet burfi and low-fat paneer. The regulator said its state-wide action has resulted in the seizure of 30 litres of liquid milk and 4,138.7 kg of milk products and sweets, including khoya, paneer, ghee, peda, halwa, shrikhand, butter and milk powder, with the total seized stock valued at ₹15,58,072. In its action against banned food products, the FDA said a joint team of its officials and police seized gutkha and other prohibited food products worth ₹95.30 lakh in Rajur, Jalna district, on September 9. The team also seized vehicles used to transport the banned products, valued at around ₹40 lakh, bringing the total value of the seized goods and vehicles to ₹1.35 crore. Police have registered a case against two individuals, Sandeep Dattu Bhumkar, Ashish Dholtani, and the supplier companies under various provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Food Safety and Standards Act, and MCOCA (Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act). In Beed district, a joint FDA-police team intercepted a Mahindra Scorpio allegedly being used to transport banned gutkha near the Barshi Naka area. Officials detained two men, Dattatray Ghodke and Omkar Ghodke, and seized gutkha worth ₹3.63 lakh and the vehicle worth ₹7 lakh. A case was registered against the two men and the supplier company under MCOCA, said the release. The FDA further said in a special drive in Mumbai on September 12, it acted against five establishments where it found prohibited food products. It seized banned food stock worth ₹20,21,100, registered one FIR and arrested nine people. The regulator also seized five vehicles allegedly used to transport the prohibited products, with their combined value at ₹98 lakh. (Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.) title: Traffic, tourism and economy among election concerns
description: Residents and business owners in Onchan discuss key concerns ahead of the House of Keys election.
content: - Published Residents and business owners in Onchan have said traffic, tourism and the cost of living are among their key concerns ahead of the 2026 House of Keys election. The constituency has the second largest population on the Isle of Man after Douglas, and sits along the east coast. Sally Hellwich, who runs a family travel business, has lived in Onchan for 30 years. She said she had 'lived, worked, and breathed Onchan" and was "sad" no candidates had considered tourism as a priority. She said: "I truly believe that tourism underpins the Isle of Man. And if we don't have tourists, we're not generating income for the economy." 'Crazy traffic' As a mother, she added that housing was another big concern for younger generations. She said: "There's not enough access to housing," adding: "Trying to get on the housing ladder now is just ridiculous." For Onchan mum Lara, speeding traffic through the town is a big worry, especially with children walking to school on their own. A rollout of more 20mph zones around the island, including near schools and residential areas, began under the previous administration. The all-island scheme started in Port Erin in 2025 after Tynwald unanimously voted in 2020 to support speed reductions in urban areas. Expanding further north, the locations were opposed by residents concerned about congestion. Lara also welcomed the introduction of more 20mph zones and said she could not understand why "there was so much resistance to it." She added that in cities like Belfast there are commonly "speed bumps on the road around schools, but they don't have any of that" on the island. Meanwhile, for Onchan business owners Dinko Matevski and Liliya Slavova, the cost of living was their biggest worry. Originally from Bulgaria, they have lived on the island for more than 14 years and have run a cafe in the town's Village Walk area for the last three. Matevski said rising stock prices were "crazy", adding that "every day our suppliers are coming with new prices and we're trying to survive". Slavova said: "We want to have staff, but we cannot afford it." In the past three years she noticed a change in customer habits too, with people cutting back their orders. "They're struggling," she said. The Isle of Man House of Keys election takes place on 24 September, with polling stations around the island open from 08:00 to 20:00 BST.

title: How hotter weather is making us poorer
description: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.
content: The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world. According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties. These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example. "Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers . How climate change is already hitting incomes A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050. But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets? "If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario. Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains. "Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW. Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price. "As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down." Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July. Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany. Compounding existing economic pressures One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output. Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024. "The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty." The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance. These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance. In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality. Can climate adaptation limit costs? "Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study. Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things." However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital to head off much worse future economic impacts. The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis. Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted. But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively. Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says. Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets. "Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

title: Hormuz Shipping Traffic Remains Stuck in Single Digits
description: Tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains a fraction of pre-war levels, with four vessels traversing the waterway on Tuesday, down from seven the previous day, Reuters has reported, citing ship-tracking data. The data does not include tankers that have t…
content: Tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains a fraction of pre-war levels, with four vessels traversing the waterway on Tuesday, down from seven the previous day, Reuters has reported, citing ship-tracking data. The data does not include tankers that have turned off their geolocation devices, the publication noted. Meanwhile, Windward reported just one tanker entering the Strait of Hormuz on September 15th—an oil product carrier. Per the data cited by Reuters, two tankers entered the chokepoint on Tuesday, and two exited. None of the four were very large crude carriers or LNG carriers, Reuters noted. One carried liquefied petroleum gas, and another was loaded with naphtha. The 10-day moving average was 18, according to the publication. Owners and energy exporters are becoming increasingly careful navigating through the Strait of Hormuz amid re-escalation of hostilities, strikes on tankers, and the relatively new threat from the Iran-aligned Houthis in the Red Sea, targeting Saudi shipments. The latest Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s vital East-West pipeline has led to crude oil loading cancelations from Yanbu. Because of the attack, there are reports that Saudi Arabia is looking to raise shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, as the Houthis have expanded their control over the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Whether that would be possible in light of the latest crossing numbers is doubtful. Reports about the length of time it would take Aramco to fix the East-West pipeline range from a few days to several weeks. The rate of tanker traffic via the Strait of Hormuz has been declining for a couple of weeks now, from 10-day moving averages of double digits to less than 10 over the past few days. Even if there are as many tankers crossing Hormuz in dark mode as there are tankers moving through it visible, rates remain severely subdued. title: Global Market: Klaas Knot tops list of potential Lagarde successors at ECB
description: France may support former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president in exchange for a French candidate getting the chief economist role, according to Reuters sources. Other names in contention include Pablo Hernández de…
content: Lagarde's current term runs until October 2027, although speculation about a possible early departure has persisted for much of this year. The succession process is therefore beginning to attract attention across the eurozone. Read more: Global Market Today: Asian stocks steady as traders await Fed decision Knot, 59, is among the leading names being discussed. A monetary economist by training, he served as president of the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025 and spent 14 years on the ECB's Governing Council, giving him extensive experience in eurozone monetary policy. Read more: US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent says rising bond yields due to 'global issues' Knot's tenure on the ECB's rate-setting body included sharply contrasting relationships with its presidents. He was initially critical of Mario Draghi's aggressive monetary stimulus, particularly as the ECB expanded its efforts to lift inflation toward its 2% target. His opposition became more public in 2019 when Draghi secured support for another stimulus package despite significant resistance among policymakers. Another potential candidate is Pablo Hernández de Cos, 55, who has headed the Bank for International Settlements since 2025. He previously served as governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024, overseeing the central bank through the pandemic, a period of exceptionally low inflation and the subsequent aggressive tightening cycle. Reuters reported that de Cos is viewed by colleagues as a pragmatic economist who relies heavily on data and research and is willing to seek compromise. Before becoming governor, he served as the Bank of Spain's chief economist, an unusual transition from a research role into senior policymaking. De Cos has also held prominent international roles, including chairing the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. His international profile increased further through his role at the BIS. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel is another possible contender. The 60-year-old economist has led Germany's central bank since 2022 and has taken a less confrontational approach toward the ECB than his predecessor Jens Weidmann. Nagel remains a moderate hawk but has generally sought to work within the ECB's policymaking framework. He has clearly articulated his policy positions while showing a willingness to compromise on other issues. Nagel has also backed the creation of a European Deposit Insurance Scheme, despite long-standing German concerns over the potential financial burden on German taxpayers. He has strongly defended the ECB's independence and criticised political pressure on the central bank. European Investment Bank President Nadia Calvino, 57, is another name that has surfaced in discussions, although she has not publicly expressed an interest in the ECB presidency. Calvino, a former Spanish cabinet minister, is not a monetary economist but has extensive experience managing large institutions. Reuters reported that her management skills and experience could be relevant to leading the ECB and its 27-member Governing Council. Gender could also become a factor in the succession discussions. There are currently only two women on the ECB's Governing Council, and both are due to leave within the next year. The eventual choice will depend on negotiations among eurozone governments, with the balance between national representation, monetary-policy experience and broader European institutional considerations likely to shape the succession process. title: How do you introduce a dog to an autistic child?
description: How To Introduce a Dog to an Autistic Child: A Comprehensive Guide Successfully introducing a dog to an autistic child requires careful planning, patience, and a deep understanding of both the child’s and the dog’s needs; How do you introduce a dog to an auti…
content: Successfully introducing a dog to an autistic child requires careful planning, patience, and a deep understanding of both the child’s and the dog’s needs; How do you introduce a dog to an autistic child? It’s achieved through gradual, structured interactions, focusing on safety, creating positive associations, and respecting boundaries to foster a beneficial and harmonious relationship. The bond between a child and a dog can be incredibly powerful, offering numerous benefits. However, for autistic children, the introduction process requires extra sensitivity and awareness. - Potential Benefits: A well-matched and well-introduced dog can provide: - Emotional support and companionship: Dogs can offer unconditional love and reduce feelings of loneliness or anxiety. - Improved social skills: Interacting with a dog can help develop communication and social skills, as children learn to interpret the dog’s body language and respond appropriately. - Sensory regulation: The tactile experience of petting a dog can be calming and provide sensory input. - Increased physical activity: Dog ownership encourages walks and playtime, promoting physical health. - Responsibility and routine: Caring for a dog can instill a sense of responsibility and help establish a daily routine. - Potential Challenges: It’s important to acknowledge the potential difficulties: - Sensory sensitivities: Autistic children may be sensitive to the dog’s barking, licking, shedding, or strong smells. - Communication difficulties: Interpreting the dog’s needs and communicating effectively can be challenging. - Unexpected behaviors: The dog’s unpredictable movements or behaviors may cause anxiety or overwhelm. - Difficulty with boundaries: Setting and maintaining appropriate boundaries with the dog may be difficult. - Hyperfocus: The child may hyperfocus on the dog, neglecting other activities or responsibilities. How do you introduce a dog to an autistic child? This requires a phased approach, prioritizing safety and comfort at every stage. - Preparation is Key: Before bringing the dog home: - Gather information: Learn about the child’s specific sensory sensitivities, communication style, and comfort levels. - Dog selection: Choose a dog with a calm, predictable temperament, ideally one that has experience with children. - Home preparation: Create a safe space for the dog, such as a crate or designated room, where it can retreat when feeling overwhelmed. - Sensory familiarization: Introduce the child to dog-related smells and sounds gradually, using recordings or scent samples. - The First Meeting: Keep the initial encounter short and controlled: - Neutral territory: If possible, arrange the first meeting in a neutral environment, such as a park, to reduce territoriality. - Leash control: Keep the dog on a leash to ensure safety and prevent chasing or jumping. - Distance: Start with a significant distance between the child and the dog, gradually decreasing it as the child feels comfortable. - Positive reinforcement: Reward the child for calm behavior and positive interactions, such as gentle petting or speaking in a quiet voice. - No pressure: Never force the child to interact with the dog. Allow them to approach at their own pace. - Introducing the Dog to the Home: Gradual acclimation to the home environment is vital: - Controlled access: Initially, limit the dog’s access to certain areas of the house, especially the child’s bedroom or personal space. - Scent exchange: Allow the child to become familiar with the dog’s scent by introducing a blanket or toy that the dog has used. - Supervised interactions: Always supervise interactions between the child and the dog, especially in the early stages. - Quiet time: Ensure the dog has plenty of quiet time to rest and adjust to its new surroundings. - Building a Relationship: Encouraging positive interactions is key for bonding: - Structured activities: Engage the child and dog in structured activities, such as playing fetch or going for short walks. - Positive reinforcement: Continue to reward both the child and the dog for positive interactions. - Teach the child: Provide clear and simple instructions on how to interact with the dog appropriately, such as gentle petting and avoiding pulling on the ears or tail. - Respect boundaries: Teach the child to respect the dog’s boundaries and recognize signs of stress or discomfort. Understanding common mistakes can improve the success of the introduction. - Rushing the process: A gradual introduction is crucial. Don’t force the child or the dog to interact before they are ready. - Ignoring sensory sensitivities: Be mindful of the child’s sensory sensitivities and avoid overwhelming them with loud noises, strong smells, or sudden movements. - Lack of supervision: Never leave the child and dog unsupervised, especially in the early stages of the relationship. - Ignoring the dog’s needs: Ensure the dog’s needs for exercise, rest, and quiet time are met. - Expecting too much too soon: Building a strong bond takes time and patience. How long should the initial meeting between the child and the dog last? The first meeting should be very brief, no more than 5-10 minutes. The goal is to create a positive first impression without overwhelming either the child or the dog. Observe their body language carefully and end the interaction before either party shows signs of stress or discomfort. What if the child is afraid of dogs? If the child is afraid of dogs, a more gradual approach is necessary. Start by exposing them to pictures or videos of dogs from a distance. Then, consider having them interact with a therapy dog or a very calm, well-trained dog in a controlled environment, with the guidance of a professional. How do you teach an autistic child to be gentle with a dog? Use simple, clear instructions and positive reinforcement. For example, you can say, “Gentle hands,” while gently guiding the child’s hand to pet the dog softly. Reward them with praise or a small treat when they interact with the dog appropriately. Role-playing can also be helpful. What are the signs that the dog is stressed or overwhelmed? Signs of stress in a dog include: panting, yawning, lip licking, whale eye (showing the whites of their eyes), tucked tail, flattened ears, and avoiding eye contact. If you observe any of these signs, immediately separate the child and the dog. What if the dog barks excessively? Excessive barking can be triggering for autistic children. Address the underlying cause of the barking, such as boredom, anxiety, or territoriality. Provide the dog with plenty of exercise, mental stimulation, and training to reduce barking. Consider consulting with a professional dog trainer or behaviorist. Can a service dog or therapy dog help an autistic child? Yes, both service dogs and therapy dogs can provide significant benefits to autistic children. Service dogs are trained to perform specific tasks to assist individuals with disabilities, such as providing deep pressure therapy or preventing wandering. Therapy dogs provide emotional support and comfort in various settings. What are the key differences between a service dog and a therapy dog? The key difference lies in their training and purpose. Service dogs are individually trained to perform specific tasks for individuals with disabilities and have legal protections under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Therapy dogs provide emotional support and comfort in various settings, but do not have the same legal protections. What should I do if the child tries to hug or kiss the dog excessively? Hugging and kissing can be overwhelming for dogs. Teach the child alternative ways to show affection, such as gentle petting, speaking in a soft voice, or offering a treat. Explain to the child that the dog prefers to be petted rather than hugged. How can I prevent the dog from jumping on the child? Train the dog to sit or stay when greeting people. Use positive reinforcement to reward the dog for calm behavior. If the dog jumps, redirect its attention to a different activity. Consistency is key to preventing jumping. What if the dog steals the child’s toys? Teach the dog the “leave it” command. When the dog attempts to take a toy, say “leave it” and offer a higher-value treat. This will teach the dog to associate leaving the toy with a positive reward. Store the child’s toys in a place where the dog cannot access them. How do you introduce a dog to an autistic child who has sensory processing issues? When introducing a dog to an autistic child with sensory processing issues, it’s important to minimize sensory overload. Keep initial interactions short and quiet, and avoid strong smells or bright lights. Gradually introduce the dog’s presence and sounds, while closely monitoring the child’s reaction. What type of training is best for a dog living with an autistic child? Focus on basic obedience training to ensure the dog is well-behaved and responsive to commands. Socialization is also crucial to help the dog become comfortable in different environments and around various people and animals. Consider working with a trainer who has experience working with dogs and autistic children.

title: Bayern make Florian Wirtz decision as Liverpool star’s future continues to be questioned
description: Bayern Munich are not currently looking to make a move on Florian Wirtz.The Germany international has been tentatively linked with the exit door at Liverpool in light of a mixed spell with the Anfield...
content: Bayern Munich are not currently looking to make a move on Florian Wirtz. The Germany international has been tentatively linked with the exit door at Liverpool in light of a mixed spell with the Anfield club following his move in 2025. However, Christian Falk reports that though the Bavarian giants remain admirers, Vincent Kompany’s men have a perfectly suitable squad. Bayern would be open to Florian Wirtz transfer We can appreciate that Bayern aren’t actively working on a deal for Florian Wirtz – and Liverpool have no interest in selling. Of course, we can simultaneously agree that were the playmaker to become available on the market, this is a conversation FC Bayern would have to involve themselves in. Falk exclusively informed CF Bayern Insider: “Of course, if Florian Wirtz were, at some point in future, interested in making a return to the Bundesliga, Bayern Munich would be the first team he’d talk to. “However, there is nothing planned. Bayern have a big squad and everyone’s feeling really confident. Musiala has a long contract and don’t forget that Vincent Kompany is trying a new system with Michael Olise as the fulcrum in the centre – the same position he currently plays in for the French national team. “So, FC Bayern have a lot of options. Don’t forget, either, that it was a lot of money Liverpool paid for Wirtz.” There is certainly always a willingness to break the bank in Munich when a player of a certain calibre becomes available and there is a clear squad need. Want more CF Bayern Insider coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust Bayern Munich proved as much with their successful pursuit of former Tottenham striker Harry Kane, who signed in an initial €100m (£86.4m) deal in 2023. Again, two years later, the Bundesliga outfit was prepared to commit a vast sum of money for the potential signing of Wirtz – only to be beaten to the punch by Arne Slot’s Liverpool. Perhaps this is one story to keep an eye on while question marks (at least, from the perspective of English media) persist over the 23-year-old. Less running, more creating for Wirtz at Liverpool It feels like a lot of Florian Wirtz’s problems at Liverpool (if they can be described as such) boil down to the wrong expectations being placed on the No.7. Should Liverpool’s most creative midfielder be covering more ground on average than Ryan Gravenberch, Dominik Szoboszlai and Alexis Mac Allister? * Stats courtesy of Fotmob from the 2026/27 Premier League season Now, there’s a clear distinction here between working hard as part of a press-heavy team under Andoni Iraola and covering for deficiencies elsewhere in the squad. While there’ll be a clear expectation for Wirtz to work hard, it shouldn’t come at the cost of his creative capabilities. This is a footballer who, when fully unleashed, can change the course of a football match at the drop of a hat. title: Takaichi Retains Core LDP Team
description: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi launched a new Liberal Democratic Party executive team on September 16, retaining most of the party’s senior leadership while pledging to unite the government and ruling party to overcome a difficult political and economic enviro…
content: TOKYO - Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi launched a new Liberal Democratic Party executive team on September 16, retaining most of the party’s senior leadership while pledging to unite the government and ruling party to overcome a difficult political and economic environment. Takaichi entered LDP headquarters at around 9:40 a.m. and attended an extraordinary General Council meeting before the party’s new leadership lineup was formally announced. "We will open the future through policy by having the party and government work as one to overcome these difficulties, until the people can truly feel prosperity and security through economic growth," Takaichi said. The reshuffle left the core of the party leadership largely unchanged. Vice President Taro Aso, Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki, Policy Research Council Chairman Takayuki Kobayashi and Election Strategy Committee Chairman Yasutoshi Nishimura were all retained. The main change was the appointment of former Diet Affairs Committee Chairman Hiroshi Kajiyama as General Council chairman. Kajiyama’s former post as Diet Affairs Committee chairman was given to former Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masafumi Murai. A senior LDP official described the lineup as a shift made with next year’s party presidential election in mind. The decision to keep many senior figures in place suggests Takaichi is prioritizing party stability and factional balance as she heads into a politically difficult autumn. The Upper House leadership also saw changes. Diet Affairs Committee Chairman Yosuke Isozaki was retained, but Secretary-General Hiroshi Ishii was not reappointed. The post will instead be taken by Hiroshi Aoki, chairman of the House of Councillors Rules and Administration Committee. The Upper House personnel process appeared to be difficult. Several lawmakers, including former General Council Chairwoman Haruko Arimura, were approached as possible successors to Ishii but declined, leaving the appointment unsettled until a late stage and raising the possibility of lingering tensions within the party. The reshuffle gives Takaichi a leadership team designed more for continuity than renewal. That may help her maintain control inside the LDP, but it also leaves her dependent on many of the same senior figures as she confronts tax, budget, monetary policy and election strategy challenges. The timing is politically sensitive. Takaichi is trying to stabilize her administration after a difficult summer dominated by the weak yen, rising bond yields, debate over household relief and questions about the government’s relationship with the Bank of Japan. The BOJ’s September 17-18 policy meeting is now the immediate test. Markets expect the central bank to raise its policy rate from 1% to 1.25%, continuing Japan’s shift away from years of ultra-low interest rates. For Takaichi, a rate hike would be both helpful and difficult. Higher rates could support the yen and help ease import-driven inflation, particularly for food, energy and raw materials. But they would also raise borrowing costs for the government, companies and households, making it harder for the administration to finance its tax cuts, defense spending and long-term investment plans. That tension has become the central political issue facing the government. Takaichi wants to present her administration as capable of helping households through higher prices while also rebuilding Japan’s industrial base through strategic investment. Markets, however, are asking whether those promises can survive in a world where government borrowing is no longer cheap. The cabinet last week approved an outline for food-tax relief and household payouts, keeping alive Takaichi’s pledge to reduce the consumption tax on food from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027. The government also plans payments that would effectively remove the remaining 1% burden for households during the period. The plan is politically important because food prices remain one of the clearest sources of voter frustration. But it is fiscally difficult. The cut is expected to create a revenue shortfall of around 5 trillion yen, and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has said the government will not rely on deficit-financing bonds to cover the cost. The funding question remains unresolved. The government has pointed to budget reforms, non-tax revenue and reviews of past inflation-relief spending, but it has not yet provided a detailed structure that would satisfy markets. That leaves the tax cut vulnerable to criticism as a promise that is politically clear but fiscally incomplete. The BOJ’s expected rate hike increases that pressure. Higher interest rates will raise debt-servicing costs, and Japan’s 10-year government bond yield has already climbed to around 3%, its highest level in roughly three decades. Takaichi has said the government will aim to cap new government bond issuance at around 40 trillion yen in the fiscal 2027 budget, but investors are likely to judge that target against actual spending needs. Those needs are rising across the government. Ministries are preparing large budget requests, defense spending remains on an expansion path, social security costs continue to grow, and Takaichi is promoting a 370 trillion yen public-private investment roadmap through fiscal 2040. The roadmap covers strategic sectors including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, shipbuilding, energy, space, quantum technology and advanced manufacturing. The yen is the immediate signal of whether markets believe that balance is credible. Its recent rally has been driven by expectations of BOJ tightening, but currency markets remain vulnerable to sharp moves if the central bank’s guidance differs from investor expectations. A stronger yen would help households by lowering import costs, but a rapid unwind of yen-funded carry trades could create market volatility. For years, investors borrowed cheaply in yen and invested in higher-yielding currencies and assets abroad. As Japanese rates rise and the yen strengthens, those trades become less attractive and may be forced to unwind. That makes Governor Kazuo Ueda’s communication after the BOJ decision as important as the rate move itself. If Ueda signals a steady path toward further hikes, the yen could strengthen and bond yields could rise further. If he sounds cautious, the yen rally could fade, reviving concerns over import inflation and weakening the political benefit of the rate hike. The BOJ must also protect its independence. Takaichi’s administration has repeatedly said that specific monetary policy tools belong to the central bank, but the broader political setting remains sensitive. Reports earlier this year that Takaichi had asked Ueda to increase government bond purchases if necessary to contain rising long-term yields have kept the issue alive. If the BOJ hikes rates this week, the government will need to show that it accepts the decision as part of inflation control, not as an obstacle to its agenda. If the administration appears to pressure the central bank over bond yields, investors may again question whether fiscal policy is constraining monetary policy. Trade data has added to the pressure. Japan recorded a trade deficit of 1.1 trillion yen in August, the fourth straight monthly deficit, as oil imports surged. Imports rose sharply from a year earlier, while exports also increased, supported by computer chips and autos. The figures underline Japan’s vulnerability to energy prices and exchange-rate movements. The trade deficit strengthens the political case for a stable yen. Japan remains heavily dependent on imported energy, and higher oil prices can quickly feed into household bills, transport costs and corporate expenses. That makes currency policy and BOJ credibility directly relevant to voters, not only to markets. At the same time, a stronger yen could weigh on exporters. Automakers and other major manufacturers benefit from a weaker currency when overseas earnings are converted into yen. Takaichi must therefore manage a divided economic constituency: households want relief from import inflation, while export industries may be more cautious about rapid yen appreciation. China remains another foreign-policy concern. Regional tensions over Taiwan, defense spending and strategic supply chains have reinforced Takaichi’s emphasis on economic security, while also raising the risk that diplomatic disputes could spill into trade and business confidence. Japan’s latest defense white paper has already generated controversy by framing military buildup not only as a security necessity but also as part of economic growth and industrial development. That message fits Takaichi’s wider strategy, but it also adds to the fiscal debate. Defense expansion, industrial policy and food-tax relief all compete for credibility in the same budget environment. The September 16 political picture is therefore dominated by two linked developments: Takaichi has secured continuity inside the LDP leadership, but she still faces a narrowing policy corridor outside the party. She needs the BOJ to be credible enough to support the yen and contain inflation, but not so aggressive that it undermines her growth and tax-relief agenda. She needs to reassure bond markets while funding household support. She needs to strengthen defense and economic security without making fiscal policy look overloaded. The central question is whether the new LDP leadership can help Takaichi maintain control through the autumn. If the BOJ’s expected rate hike stabilizes the yen, if bond yields remain manageable and if the government explains the food-tax funding plan, the administration may regain some momentum. If higher rates push yields up further, unsettle markets or expose gaps in the tax-cut plan, the leadership reshuffle may be seen less as a fresh start than as an effort to hold the party together before a difficult policy fight.
